headline: Industrial Waste Lagoon Carved into Iowa’s Loess Hills Without Public Notice
deck: A five-acre excavation site appeared overnight near a historic cemetery, revealing plans to store meat-processing waste that bypassed regulators and alarmed locals.
body: A dirt pit the size of five football fields materialized in under a week next to Center Cemetery in Castana, Iowa, catching residents and officials completely off guard. The excavation sits on the edge of the Loess Hills, a 200-mile stretch of craggy bluffs and ridges that form one of the state’s most ecologically sensitive landscapes. For weeks, locals could only trade rumors about a private developer building a lagoon to hold animal-waste byproducts from a meat-processing plant 50 miles away in Sioux City. Alison Manz, an Iowa Department of Natural Resources (DNR) field officer, received four complaints about the construction in late June—complaints her office had no prior knowledge of. 'It was just sort of a rumor,' said Scott Koepsell, whose family owns farmland less than a mile from the site. 'But we didn’t know for sure…and we had no good answers.'

State records later confirmed the project’s purpose. Brian Gallup of Hawthorn Land Holdings told Manz the company was developing a solid waste pit to store 'industrial byproduct waste' from Seaboard Triumph Foods’ pork processing facility in Sioux City. The plan involves applying the waste as fertilizer to nearby farmland at a rate of less than two tons per acre per year—a threshold that avoids triggering Iowa’s permitting requirements for solid waste and sludge. Hawthorn Land Holdings has not publicly disclosed the lagoon’s capacity or the full scope of the industrial byproducts it intends to store. 'I started checking around because we didn’t know anything about it,' said Monona County Supervisor Bo Fox. Fox only learned of the lagoon after a panicked resident whose land borders the site reached out to him directly.

The Loess Hills corridor is a critical environmental and cultural landmark in western Iowa, known for its steep ridges, rare prairie ecosystems, and proximity to the Missouri River valley. Any industrial activity in the area—especially one involving untreated animal waste—carries outsized risks for groundwater contamination and soil degradation. Iowa’s DNR has no record of a public consultation process for the project, and local officials say they were left in the dark until after construction began. 'We didn’t have any idea this was happening,' said Fox. 'If this is legal under current rules, then those rules need to change.'

Hawthorn Land Holdings’ decision to proceed without permits or public notice underscores a broader pattern in Iowa, where industrial agriculture operations often expand with minimal regulatory oversight. The state’s rules for solid waste application allow companies to bypass permitting by keeping application rates below two tons per acre per year, even for industrial byproducts that may contain pathogens, heavy metals, or pharmaceutical residues. Environmental advocates argue that this loophole enables companies to sidestep scrutiny while potentially poisoning soil and water. 'The fact that they can do this without a permit is outrageous,' said one local farmer who asked to remain anonymous. 'What’s next? They’ll start dumping who knows what on our land?'

Seaboard Triumph Foods, one of the largest pork processors in the country, has not publicly commented on its connection to the lagoon. The company, which operates a massive facility in Sioux City, processes tens of thousands of hogs daily, generating vast quantities of wastewater and solid waste. While the specifics of the waste stream stored in the Castana lagoon remain unclear, industry experts warn that even treated byproducts can pose significant environmental risks if not managed properly. 'These are not benign materials,' said an environmental engineer who reviewed the project details but asked not to be named. 'Even at low application rates, cumulative impacts over time can be severe.'

Residents are now scrambling to understand the implications. The site’s proximity to Center Cemetery—a historic burial ground—and its location within the Loess Hills’ fragile ecosystem has amplified concerns. Koepsell and others fear the lagoon could leach contaminants into groundwater or release noxious odors during decomposition. 'This isn’t just some abandoned pit in the middle of nowhere,' Koepsell said. 'People come to this area for its natural beauty and quiet. Now we’re looking at a potential environmental disaster.'

Bo Fox has called a town hall meeting for July 14 to address the community’s questions and pressure state regulators to intervene. 'We need answers,' Fox said. 'And we need them fast.' Meanwhile, Iowa DNR officials have pledged to review the project’s compliance with state rules, but have not indicated whether they will halt construction or require additional permits. The agency’s delayed response has only deepened residents’ mistrust. 'They’re supposed to protect us, not rubber-stamp these kinds of projects,' said another local resident. 'What good is a permit system if companies can just bypass it?'

The lagoon’s sudden appearance highlights a troubling lack of transparency in Iowa’s industrial waste management practices. Without public notice or environmental impact assessments, communities are left to react to faits accomplis rather than shape decisions that affect their land, water, and health. As Fox put it during a recent county board meeting, 'We’re not against development. But this? This feels like a violation.'
